Pages are not categorized or tagged, but can have a hierarchy. You can nest pages under other pages by making one the “Parent” of the other, creating a group of pages.

/how-it-works/.visibleText:
How it works

Radio settings

It’s 2 AM.
The power’s out, and so is cell service.

A scenario, not a real event. It shows how the system is meant to work.

The phones go quiet. Ice brings the lines down overnight. At a warming shelter, a resident’s home oxygen concentrator has no power.
A volunteer picks up the radio. The shelter’s ACS operator writes an ICS-213 and reads it, word for word, to net control on W7GBU.
The radio room copies it. Another volunteer copies the message, logs it on an ICS-309 and hands it to the county’s Emergency Operations Center.
The EOC acts on it. The request moves through the agency’s own channels. By morning it’s handled, and every hop is on paper.

Radio still works. Because people practice.

The weekly net

A net is an on-air meeting. Ours is a directed net: net control calls each group in turn, so everyone gets heard.

Every Tuesday, 8:00 PM

What happens, in order

Net control opens the net; emergency or priority traffic may break in at any time.
Officials check in.
Members check in.
Visitors check in.
Visiting? Wait for the call for visitors. Give your call sign slowly and phonetically, then your name and location. Not licensed? Just listen.
Simplex, no-tone and cross-band stations, then relays.
Traffic and late check-ins, then net control closes the net.
Other nets
Winlink nights: 2nd and 4th Tuesdays; net control gives a Winlink assignment during the net.
Fifth Tuesdays: the net starts on simplex, then moves to W7GBU.
ACS GMRS net: 3rd Tuesdays, 7:30 PM, for county volunteers with GMRS licenses.
When the county calls

The county activates ACS members; ARES members serve events and the National Weather Service without a call-out. ARES and ACS

It has happened for real: in the Gray and Oregon Road fires of August 2023, the group provided a mobile network unit for the incident command post and the Disaster Assistance Center.

Request. The county needs radio support.
Mission number. The county gets a state mission number, which ties the activation to Washington’s emergency-worker protections.
Activation message. It goes to members registered for notices.
Check in. Available members check in with net control on W7GBU.
Assignment. Go to your assignment or a staging area.
Release. Served agencies and the emergency coordinator release members.
Review. Once every station is secured and home, leaders hold an action review within 72 hours.
Readiness levels

Four levels tell members what to do. This site never shows a current level.

Inactive

Green

Normal conditions

Normal operations. Check and recharge batteries monthly.

Alert

Yellow

Something might happen

Check radios, go-kits and supplies. Watch National Weather Service statements.

Stand by

Orange

Something has happened

Load your go-kit. Monitor NOAA Weather Radio WXL86 (162.400 MHz) and W7GBU.

Deploy

Red

Full activation

Follow the activation steps above.

When no one has called yet

If communications fail and there are no instructions, the Eastern Washington Section’s Standing Order 1b applies. Safety comes first: no one is asked to leave home or travel. Then send a Washington State Field Situation Report by Winlink.

Read Standing Order 1b
(opens ag7qp.com)

How a message moves

If W7GBU is down, messages move by the alternate repeater, simplex (radio to radio), HF radio or Winlink.

Forms and logs

The ICS-213 is the Incident Command System’s standard message form. It travels by voice, on paper or inside Winlink. Keep it short: To, From, Subject, Date, Time, the message and who approved it. The reply goes on the same form.

Precedence: Emergency, then Priority, Welfare and Routine.

ICS-309 communications log: every message sent or received. Winlink Express can build it.
ICS-214 activity log: what you did and when.
Winlink

Winlink is email by radio, with forms and attachments. It works with or without the internet. State and USGS forms are built in; reports can be plotted on a map. The group runs its own gateway, W7GBU-10.

ARES

What we are not

Not first responders. We support the agencies that respond.

History and W7GBU
The W7GBU story

Our call sign honors Ira “Dean” Bula, W7GBU. For years he handed out technical wisdom and friendly advice from the counter at Northwest Electronics. Each morning he led an on-air round table on the repeater that now carries his call. Newly licensed hams found him there, and it became the 7:30 Bunch, which still meets weekday mornings. When the county retired the repeater’s old call sign, the Spokane County ARES-RACES Support Group applied for Dean’s call to inspire its members.

“He was a person who made a difference in Spokane by making others feel like they could make a difference themselves.”

How it works

Radio settings

It’s 2 AM.
The power’s out, and so is cell service.

A scenario, not a real event. It shows how the system is meant to work.

The phones go quiet. Ice brings the lines down overnight. At a warming shelter, a resident’s home oxygen concentrator has no power.
A volunteer picks up the radio. The shelter’s ACS operator writes an ICS-213 and reads it, word for word, to net control on W7GBU.
The radio room copies it. Another volunteer copies the message, logs it on an ICS-309 and hands it to the county’s Emergency Operations Center.
The EOC acts on it. The request moves through the agency’s own channels. By morning it’s handled, and every hop is on paper.

ARES and ACS

ARES

Amateur Radio Emergency Service

The ARRL’s volunteer program, open to any licensed ham.

ACS

Auxiliary Communications

Spokane County Emergency Management’s volunteer radio unit, open to ARES members who pass a Sheriff’s Office background check.

RACES

The FCC’s rule for amateurs serving government (97.407). The county’s RACES program is now part of ACS, so older documents say “ARES/RACES.”

AUXCOMM

The federal qualification ACS is modeled on, not a separate group to join.

What we are not

Not first responders. We support the agencies that respond.
Not a replacement for 911 or the county’s radio systems.
Not a public alert service. For alerts, register with ALERT Spokane
(opens spokanecounty.gov)
.
Not a source of official incident information.
The legal basis, in plain English
Layer	Rule	What it means
Federal	47 CFR Part 97
(opens ecfr.gov)
	Every member holds an FCC license.
Federal	97.407, RACES
(opens ecfr.gov)
	Agency-certified operators, civil-defense traffic only, drills capped at one hour a week (more with approval).
State	RCW 38.52
(opens leg.wa.gov)
 and WAC 118-04
(opens leg.wa.gov)
	Emergency-worker registration and coverage.
County	Spokane County emergency plan, 2021	ACS supports ESF-2, the county’s communications function.
The rules we operate under

What this means for you. Protection comes from being a registered county emergency worker (the ACS path) on an activity with a state mission number. ARES-only activities, such as community events, are not county activations.

Who we serve
Spokane County Emergency Management: primary; activates ACS.
National Weather Service, Spokane: SKYWARN.
Area hospitals: backup communications.
Community event organizers.
Agreements
Inland Empire VHF Radio Amateurs (IEVHFRA), MOU Revision 5 (May 6, 2023): a backup repeater, a second repeater for special nets, and packet paths into Winlink.
National, through the ARRL: FEMA (2023), American Red Cross (renewed 2021), NWS SKYWARN (1986).

Joining
No membership dues.
Members use their own radios, any brand. You need nothing to visit.
ARES

History and W7GBU
The W7GBU story

Our call sign honors Ira “Dean” Bula, W7GBU. For years he handed out technical wisdom and friendly advice from the counter at Northwest Electronics. Each morning he led an on-air round table on the repeater that now carries his call. Newly licensed hams found him there, and it became the 7:30 Bunch, which still meets weekday mornings. When the county retired the repeater’s old call sign, the Spokane County ARES-RACES Support Group applied for Dean’s call to inspire its members.

“He was a person who made a difference in Spokane by making others feel like they could make a difference themselves.”
